To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the more members of a high-status group endorse an ideology that legitimates status differences, the more likely these members are to attribute negative experiences of low-status group members to discrimination, and the more members of the low-status group endorse an individual mobility ideology, the less likely these members are, in turn, to attribute negative experiences to discrimination.

the more members of lower status groups believe that individuals can change their group status, the less they attribute their negative intergroup encounters to discrimination, and the more members of higher status groups believe that status is determined by individual merit, the more they attribute the negative intergroup encounters of lower status group members as a result of discrimination.

the more members of the low-status group endorse individual mobility, relative to the more members of a high-status group endorse it, the less likely members of the low status group are to attribute discrimination in intergroup interactions to discrimination, and the more likely members of the high status group are to do so.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of legitimizing ideologies in the perception of discrimination.
understanding when members of high- and low-status groups perceive discrimination.
the role of legitimizing ideologies and relative group status in attributions to discrimination and the implications of this research for the study of intergroup relations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the status-legitimation hypothesis is not supported for all groups, but that it is supported for the majority of groups.

group members are more likely to attribute negative outcomes to discrimination when the ideology of individualism is endorsed by the high-status group, and when the ideology of group mobility is endorsed by the low-status group.

the more members of the low-status group believe that they have the ability to change their status through their own efforts, the more likely it is that they will perceive that discrimination is the cause of negative intergroup outcomes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
group status and ideology interact to determine the likelihood that members of low status groups will attribute negative outcomes from members of high status groups to discrimination.
the status of a group is a critical factor in how group members perceive discrimination.

the status-legitimation hypothesis is a useful framework for explaining the conditions under which low-status group members perceive discrimination and the conditions under which high-status group members perceive that low-status group members receive preferential treatment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
group status and ideology interact in complex ways to influence how people perceive discrimination.
group status and legitimization of inequality are important factors in understanding how members of high- and low-status groups perceive and react to intergroup discrimination.

the status-legitimation hypothesis provides a framework for understanding the role of group status in the perception of personal discrimination and for understanding how ideologies of group status differences can be used to justify discrimination against outgroup members.
